G3A01: More sunspots = more ionizing radiation = a denser ionosphere, so the higher HF bands open more often.
G3A02: A sudden ionospheric disturbance thickens the D region, which absorbs lower frequencies most. Higher bands get through better.
G3A03: Flare radiation travels at the speed of light, so it reaches Earth in about 8 minutes.
G3A04: With few sunspots, the ionosphere is too thin to bend the high bands back: 15, 12 and 10 meters are the least reliable.
G3A05: Solar flux is the Sun's radio noise measured at a wavelength of 10.7 cm (2800 MHz). Higher flux = better high-band conditions.
G3A06: A geomagnetic storm is a temporary disturbance of Earth's magnetic field, usually from a CME or solar wind stream.
G3A07: 20 meters is the dependable band: it supports worldwide daytime contacts at any point in the solar cycle.
G3A08: Geomagnetic storms hit the polar regions hardest, so high-latitude HF paths degrade.
G3A09: Storms make auroras, and auroras can reflect VHF signals.
G3A10: The Sun turns once about every 27 days, so active regions come back around on a 26 to 28 day cycle.
G3A11: A CME is a cloud of particles, much slower than light: 15 hours to several days to arrive.
G3A12: K-index = short-term (3-hour) stability of Earth's magnetic field. K for quicK.
G3A13: A-index = long-term (daily average) stability of Earth's magnetic field.
G3A14: Coronal hole particles disturb Earth's magnetic field, and that disturbs HF.
G3B01: Long path takes a longer route around the Earth and arrives a moment later, so you may hear a slight echo.
G3B02: MUF depends on path distance and location, time of day and season, and solar radiation and disturbances. All of these.
G3B03: Just below the MUF: the highest frequency that still comes back, and higher frequencies are absorbed less.
G3B04: Automated receiving networks on the internet show where your signal is actually being heard.
G3B05: Between the LUF and MUF is the usable window: those signals are refracted back to Earth.
G3B06: Below the LUF, signals are absorbed (mostly by the D region) before they reach the other station.
G3B07: LUF = Lowest Usable Frequency between two specific points.
G3B08: MUF = Maximum Usable Frequency between two points.
G3B09: One F2 hop covers up to about 2,500 miles, because F2 is the highest region.
G3B10: One E region hop covers up to about 1,200 miles. E is lower than F2, so shorter hops.
G3B11: If the LUF is above the MUF, there is no usable window: no ordinary skywave on that path.
G3B12: Summer thunderstorms make lots of static on the lower HF bands.
G3C01: From the ground up: D, E, F1, F2. D is closest to Earth.
G3C02: Critical frequency = the highest frequency that still gets refracted back at that angle.
G3C03: F2 is the highest region, so the bounce comes down farthest away.
G3C04: Critical angle = the highest takeoff angle that still comes back. Aim any steeper and the signal goes through.
G3C05: In daylight the D region forms and absorbs the low bands (160 to 40 meters), so long distance on them waits for night.
G3C06: Scatter signals arrive over many paths at once, so they sound fluttery.
G3C07: Scatter energy reaches you by several different paths at once, which distorts it.
G3C08: Only a small part of the energy gets scattered into the skip zone, so the signals are weak.
G3C09: Scatter lets you hear stations in your skip zone (too far for ground wave, too close for skywave).
G3C10: NVIS = short-range HF sent nearly straight up (high angle) and reflected straight back down.
G3C11: The D region absorbs signals below about 10 MHz during the day.
